json.summary: A bearded hipster-looking young man asks his grandmother about Grandpa Tibor's oilcloth satchel from his butterfly-collecting kit. She sends him to the shed. She cheerfully explains that the mess in there only looks like a place where a bomb went off, that it's really a brilliant system, and hands him Tibor's photo to help him 'tune in'. Shouting from inside the shed, the grandson finds a helicopter turbine and then the dried mummy of a Caucasian man, with the organs kept in an aquarium and the heart in a jam jar. Granny calmly calls it a 'property dispute' and says her Tibor was a precise man. The joke is that the late grandpa apparently killed a neighbour over a land dispute and preserved him like one of his butterfly specimens, while the sweet old lady treats it as an ordinary family quirk and swears more casually than her horrified grandson.

characters.name: grandson
characters.description: Young man with a big black beard, an undercut with a top-knot/quiff and a T-shirt (hipster look). He calls the old woman 'Nagyikám' (my granny), so he is her grandson. He has come for his late grandfather's butterfly-collecting gear. At first he speaks politely, then switches to panicked, heavy swearing when he discovers the mummy (ÁÁÁ!!! BASSZAMEG… BAZMEG!!!, FÚJBAZMEG!). In panels p2–p4 he is off-panel inside the shed.

characters.name: grandma
characters.description: Plump old woman with huge wild curly white hair and round glasses, sitting in an armchair. She is the widow of 'Tibor papa'. She is calm, cheerful and matter-of-fact, and swears casually ('kibaszott kupleráj') as if it were nothing. She speaks fondly of her husband ('Tiborom') and plays down the horrific find with a curt, euphemistic 'TELEKVITA'.

characters.name: grandpa Tibor (Tibor papa?)
characters.description: The late grandfather, named in the dialogue. He never speaks. He appears only in the framed photo grandma holds up in p1: a bald man with a moustache and glasses. He was a butterfly collector and a 'precise man' who kept his shed in an obsessive 'system', and apparently he preserved a human body there.

panels.description: Grandma sits in her armchair while the bearded grandson stands and asks about Tibor papa's satchel (r0, tail to grandson). Grandma answers that it's in the shed (r1, tail to her). The grandson sighs 'Ó jaj...' (r2, tail to him).
Grandma holds up a framed photo of bald, mustachioed Tibor while explaining the shed's 'system' (r3, tail to grandma). The grandson reaches for the photo.

Grandma alone in her armchair. The grandson's question about a helicopter turbine (r4) comes from off-panel, with its tail running along the wall/doorway at the right. Grandma answers that the stairs start behind it (r5, tail to her).
A huge jagged scream bubble (r6) comes from the off-panel grandson in the shed. Grandma calmly says 'TELEKVITA' (r7, tail to her).

The off-panel grandson describes the organs in an aquarium and the heart in a jam jar (r9). Grandma raises a finger approvingly and says 'Tiborom precíz ember volt!' (r10+r11, tail to her). r8 is an empty region.

notes: r10 and r11 are one sentence split across the bubble layout: 'TIBOROM PRECÍZ EMBER VOLT!' = 'My Tibor was a precise man!'. Translate them together and split the result across the two regions. 'Tiborom' ('my Tibor') is affectionate and possessive.

Main punchline: r7 'TELEKVITA' literally means 'land/property-boundary dispute'. It is a typical Hungarian neighbour feud over plot lines. Grandma uses it as a dry one-word explanation of why there is a mummified man in the shed: Grandpa settled a boundary dispute with his neighbour by killing and preserving him. Keep it short and deadpan, e.g. 'Boundary dispute.' or 'Property line dispute.'

Running logic: Tibor papa was a butterfly collector ('lepkegyűjtő', r0). Drying specimens and preserving parts in jars are collector or taxidermist techniques, now applied to a human (r6, r9). His 'precision' (r10–r11) is the dark payoff.

r0 'viaszosvászon tarisznya' = an oilcloth/waxed-canvas satchel or shoulder bag, an old-fashioned piece of field gear. 'Tibor papa' = Grandpa Tibor ('papa' here means grandpa). 'Nagyikám' = 'my granny', affectionate.
r1 'sufni' = colloquial word for a garden shed or lean-to storage hut. Use 'the shed'.

r3: 'kibaszott kupleráj' = 'fucking shambles'. 'Kupleráj' is slang for a mess or chaos (originally 'brothel'). '...amiben bomba robbant' = 'where a bomb went off'. The humour is that the sweet granny swears casually while defending the chaos as 'actually a genius system'. 'A ráhangolódásban segít a fényképe' = 'his photo helps you tune in / get on his wavelength', a mock-spiritual suggestion to channel the dead man's mindset.
r4–r5: absurd shed contents. There is a helicopter turbine, and 'the stairs start behind it', so the shed has hidden depths and a basement. The deadpan tone escalates toward the horror.
r5 'LÉPCSÖ' is the handwritten form of 'lépcső' (stairs). It is not a joke, so ignore the spelling.

r6: 'ÁÁÁ!!! BASSZAMEG' and 'BAZMEG!!!' are spelled-out forms of 'baszd meg' ('fuck it/fuck me'), the most common Hungarian swear-interjection. In r9 it is fused into 'FÚJBAZMEG!' ('ew-fuck!', from 'fúj' = 'yuck'). The grandson's swearing tic recurs in r6 (twice) and r9. Use strong English equivalents ('FUCK!', 'fucking hell', 'eww, fuck!').

r6 'egy kaukázusi férfi szárított múmiája' = 'the dried mummy of a Caucasian male'. The phrasing parodies police or forensic jargon ('Caucasian male'), which is funny because he is screaming in panic yet uses a clinical description.

r9: 'Fúj!... a belső szervei itt áznak egy akváriumban, a szív külön egy lekváros üvegben!' = 'Ew!... his internal organs are soaking in an aquarium here, the heart separately in a jam jar!'. The domestic containers (aquarium, jam jar) are the gross-out joke and set up 'precise man'.
Contrast gag: the grandson looks like a tough, bearded hipster but panics and swears in horror, while the tiny old granny stays serene and proud of her husband.
There are no background signs in this strip.
